Handling missing observations and censoring

Source: vignettes/articles/missing-data.qmd

Longitudinal tumor growth studies frequently involve missing observations and informative dropout. For example, animals with large tumors may be removed from a study when their tumor volumes exceed a predefined threshold.

Consequently, simply averaging the observed tumor volumes at each time point may produce misleading growth trajectories, as the remaining subjects may no longer be representative of the original study population.

The tumr package provides visualization methods designed to handle missing observations and censoring in longitudinal tumor growth data.

Data preprocessing

Before computing tumor growth summaries, the data are preprocessed using the following steps:

Aligning time points across subjects

Missing rows are introduced for unobserved time points so that all subjects share a common time grid. This allows tumor measurements to be compared consistently across subjects at each time point.

Handling trailing missing values due to censoring

When observations are missing after the last recorded measurement, the last observed value is carried forward and marked with a + to indicate right-censoring.

For example:

3, 6, 9, NA → 3, 6, 9, 9+

The carried-forward value is treated as a censored observation rather than an additional observed tumor measurement.

Interpolating embedded missing values

Missing observations occurring between two recorded measurements are estimated using linear interpolation to preserve the continuity of individual growth trajectories.

For example, at equally spaced time points:

3, NA, 9 → 3, 6, 9

Estimating tumor growth summaries

After preprocessing, tumor volume summaries can be estimated at each time point within each treatment group using a Kaplan–Meier approach. This nonparametric method incorporates censoring information into the estimation of tumor volume distributions.

library(tumr)
data("melanoma2")
melanoma2$months <- melanoma2$Day / (365 / 12)
mel2 <- tumr(melanoma2, ID, months, Volume, Treatment)
plot(mel2, par = FALSE, fold = FALSE)
plot(mel2, par = FALSE, fold = FALSE, panel = TRUE)

Although the nonparametric approach has certain advantages, it may not capture the underlying growth trend as accurately as a parametric approach in some applications. Therefore, the examples in the Getting started guide focus primarily on parametric visualization.
